title: Small projects: merging documents and roles safely
blurb: Slim PRINCE2 down for a small project by merging documents, combining roles and lightening reports, without breaking the rules.
question: On a small, low-value project, the director suggests merging the project brief and business case and being both executive and project manager. Which of these is acceptable tailoring?

teach.body: Formally, a small project still applies all seven principles, but it can tailor processes, roles, management products and controls to its size. In plain English, a small project uses a pocket-sized PRINCE2: fewer documents, fewer people wearing more hats, lighter reporting and a short lifecycle. What it cannot do is skip a principle or break the role rules that keep decisions safe.

teach.h: What can shrink on a small project
head: Area
Small-project tailoring
rows: Merge project brief and business case
PM also team manager and project support
teach.caption: Each choice is documented and agreed in the PID like any other tailoring.

teach.h: Merging the brief and business case
teach.body: On a small, low-value project, the project brief and the business case can be merged into one simple business case document. In plain English, there is no need for two documents saying much the same thing about a small piece of work. The project still needs a business justification; it is simply written up in one place.

teach.h: Why the rules do not shrink
teach.body: The role rules protect governance. One executive keeps a single point of accountability. Keeping the executive apart from the project manager means the person running the work is not also the person judging whether it is worth doing. Assurance independent of the project manager gives the board an honest view. A small project needs these checks as much as a large one; it just needs fewer people to provide them.

items.label: One simple business case (merged with the brief)
Brief highlight reports to the board
Closing a project, inside the final stage

teach.caption: The minimum is two management stages: initiation plus one delivery stage. Closure happens within the final stage, not as a stage of its own.

teach.body: Larkspur Community Theatre is replacing its box-office software, a ten-week project. Artistic director Ruth Ellison is executive. Sam Adeyemi is project manager and also acts as team manager and keeps the logs as project support. A trustee who is not on the board provides assurance. The brief and business case are one short document, there are two stages, and Ruth receives a fortnightly one-page highlight email.

teach.caption: Depending on scale, complexity, skill and capacity, the PM may also do the team manager and project support roles.

teach.text: However small the project, the executive and project manager roles are never combined, and project assurance never sits with the project manager or project support. Also, small projects still close properly: closing a project runs inside the final stage, not as a separate stage.

items: Small, low-value projects can merge the project brief and business case into one simple business case (5.4.5).
The PM may also perform the team manager and project support roles.
Executive and PM are not combined; assurance is not done by the PM, team members or support.
Minimum two stages: initiation plus one delivery stage; closure sits within the final stage.
Reporting can be lighter in frequency and formality, but the board still receives it.

summary: You can now tailor PRINCE2 for a small project: merging the project brief and business case, letting the project manager also act as team manager and project support, using two stages and lighter reporting. You can also explain why the executive and project manager roles stay separate and assurance stays independent.

A.q: On a small, low-value project, which two documents may be merged into one simple business case document?
options: The project plan and business case
The lessons report and business case
The project brief and business case
The issue register and business case
A.why: Small, low-value projects may merge the project brief and business case into one simple business case document (5.4.5).

whyNot.0: The project plan is a separate plan in the PID; the recognized merger is brief and business case.
whyNot.1: The lessons report passes on lessons at stage or project end; it is not merged with the business case.
whyNot.3: The issue register is a record in the project log, not part of the business case.

A.q: Which pair of roles must NOT be combined, however small the project?
options: Project manager and team manager
Project manager and project support
Two people sharing the senior user role
Executive and project manager
A.why: The executive role cannot be combined with the project manager role on any PRINCE2 project (6.2.4).

whyNot.0: The PM may also perform the team manager role, depending on scale and capacity.
whyNot.1: The PM may also perform the project support role, depending on scale and capacity.
whyNot.2: The senior user role can be held by more than one person.

A.q: A small, simple project has well-understood products. What is the fewest number of management stages it can have?
options: A single delivery stage
Initiation plus one delivery stage
Initiation plus two delivery stages
Starting up plus one delivery stage
A.why: Every PRINCE2 project has at least two management stages: initiation plus at least one delivery stage (7.2.3.1).

whyNot.0: An initiation stage is always needed, so one delivery stage on its own is too few.
whyNot.2: Two delivery stages are allowed but are not the minimum.
whyNot.3: Starting up a project is a pre-project process, not a management stage.

B.q: On a small project, the project manager also performs the team manager and project support roles. Which statement is correct?
options: This is allowed, depending on scale and the PM's capacity
This breaks the rule that the PM role is not shared
This is allowed for team manager, not for project support
This needs project support to take on project assurance
B.why: Depending on scale, complexity, skill and capacity, the PM may also perform the team manager and project support roles (6.2.4).

whyNot.1: Not sharing the PM role means one person holds it; that person may still take on other roles.
whyNot.2: Both combinations are allowed; project support is one of them.
whyNot.3: Project support must be kept separate from project assurance.

B.q:
Which two are appropriate tailoring choices for a small, low-risk project?
1. Merging the project brief and business case.
2. Shorter, less frequent highlight reports.
3. Having the project manager carry out project assurance.
4. Leaving out the initiation stage.
options: 2 and 3
1 and 4
1 and 2
3 and 4
B.why: Merging the brief and business case and lightening reporting are both proportionate tailoring for a small project (5.4.5, 2.7).

whyNot.0: Statement 3 is false: project assurance cannot be assigned to the project manager.
whyNot.1: Statement 4 is false: every project has an initiation stage plus at least one delivery stage.
whyNot.3: Both are false: assurance must be independent of the PM, and initiation is required.

B.q: Who can carry out project assurance on a small project?
options: The project manager, who knows the work
A board member or a person from the business
Project support, who keeps the registers
A team member, who builds the products
B.why: Assurance can be done by board members, by people appointed from the business, or externally; it cannot be the PM, team members or project support (6.2.4).

whyNot.0: Project assurance cannot be assigned to the project manager.
whyNot.2: Project support must be kept separate from project assurance.
whyNot.3: Project assurance cannot be assigned to team members.

C.q: A small charity project merges its project brief and business case, and the project manager also acts as team manager. Which statement is correct?
options: Both are acceptable tailoring for a small project
The merger is acceptable; the role combination is not
The role combination is acceptable; the merger is not
Neither is acceptable without business layer consent
C.why: Small projects may merge the brief and business case (5.4.5), and the PM may also perform the team manager role (6.2.4).

whyNot.1: The PM may also be team manager, so the role combination is acceptable too.
whyNot.2: Merging the brief and business case is recognized tailoring for small, low-value projects.
whyNot.3: Both are normal tailoring, documented in the PID and approved by the project board.

C.q: A finance director says that, as the project is tiny, she will be both executive and project manager. What should happen?
options: She takes both roles as tailoring for the project's size
She takes both roles once project assurance is strengthened
She becomes PM, and the board shares the executive role
She stays executive, and someone else becomes the PM
C.why: The executive and project manager roles cannot be combined, so a separate project manager is needed (6.2.4).

whyNot.0: Size does not change this role rule; combining them is not valid tailoring.
whyNot.1: Stronger assurance does not make combining executive and PM acceptable.
whyNot.2: There is one executive; the role cannot be shared across the board.

C.q: How is closure handled on a small project with initiation plus one delivery stage?
options: Closing is skipped once the products are delivered
Closing is a separate short stage of its own
Closing a project runs within the delivery stage
Closing is handed to the business layer to run
C.why: Closure activities are planned within the final stage, so closing a project runs inside the one delivery stage (ch 19).

whyNot.0: Closing a project must still be run, even if tailored to the situation.
whyNot.1: Closure is part of the final stage, not a management stage of its own.
whyNot.3: The project manager runs closing a project; the board then authorizes closure.

reteach.title: A pocket-sized PRINCE2
reteach.question: If PRINCE2 for a large project is a full toolbox, what goes into the pocket version for a small one, and what must still be in there?

blocks.body: The pocket version has one simple business case instead of a brief plus a business case, a project manager who also runs the team and keeps the logs, two stages, and short reports. It still has an executive who is not the project manager, independent assurance, all seven principles and a proper close at the end of the final stage.

blocks.text: Combining roles has limits: executive with PM, or assurance with PM or support, is never allowed, whatever the project's size.

explain.body: Small, low-value projects can merge the project brief and the business case into a single simple business case document. Justification is still needed; it is just written once.

test.q: Why can a small project merge its project brief and business case?
options: Its low value and simplicity suit one simple document
Its business case is not needed on a small project
Its brief is written by the business layer instead
Its PID replaces both of them during starting up
test.why: For small, low-value projects, one simple business case document can do the job of both (5.4.5).

whyNot.1: Every PRINCE2 project needs business justification; the business case is merged, not dropped.
whyNot.2: The project brief is prepared within starting up a project, not by the business layer.
whyNot.3: The PID is assembled in initiating a project, after starting up.

explain.body: The PM may also perform the team manager and project support roles, depending on scale, complexity, skill and capacity. The PM cannot also be executive or project assurance.

explain.h: Who can the PM also be?

test.q: Which role may the project manager also perform on a small project?
options: Project assurance
Project support
Executive
Business layer
test.why: The PM may also perform the project support role (and the team manager role), depending on scale and capacity (6.2.4).

whyNot.0: Project assurance cannot be assigned to the project manager.
whyNot.2: The executive role cannot be combined with the project manager.
whyNot.3: The business layer sits outside the project management team and is not a project role.

explain.body: Reports and reviews can be less frequent and less formal on a small project. The board still needs time-driven highlight reports during the stage; exceptions are still raised only when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded.

test.q: Which reporting change is appropriate tailoring for a small, low-risk project?
options: Highlight reports dropped until the stage ends
Less frequent, shorter highlight reports
Exception reports for every small variance
Reporting to the business layer, not the board
test.why: Tailoring adjusts the frequency and formality of reports; shorter, less frequent highlight reports suit a small, low-risk project (2.7).

whyNot.0: Time-driven reporting to the board is still needed in every stage.
whyNot.2: Exception reports are for forecast breaches of stage tolerance, not every small variance.
whyNot.3: Highlight reports go to the project board, which directs the project.

explain.body: All seven principles, the role rules, an initiation stage and a proper close in the final stage apply on every PRINCE2 project, however small.

test.q: Which still applies on even the smallest PRINCE2 project?
options: A separate team manager role
At least three management stages
A separate brief and business case
All seven PRINCE2 principles
test.why: All seven principles must be applied for any project to be a PRINCE2 project (ch 2).

whyNot.0: The team manager role is optional; the PM may do it.
whyNot.1: The minimum is two stages: initiation plus one delivery stage.
whyNot.2: Small, low-value projects may merge the brief and business case.
